concept: Parkinson's disease motor drug therapy: levodopa, dopamine agonists, MAO-B/COMT/A2A drugs, fluctuations, dyskinesia, gait and medication safety

claims.text: Punding is a related repetitive, non-goal-directed behaviour, such as repeatedly sorting, assembling or disassembling objects; it and DDS are related to, but distinguishable from, the usual gambling, shopping, eating and sexual ICDs. (medium confidence)
Rytary is an oral extended-release carbidopa-levodopa capsule; its beads dissolve and are absorbed at different rates. (medium confidence)
Levodopa is the principal pharmacological approach for troublesome Parkinsonian tremor; it can improve both resting and action tremor, although individual response varies. (medium confidence)
CREXONT contains immediate-release carbidopa/levodopa granules and extended-release levodopa pellets, combining rapid and sustained delivery within an oral capsule. (high confidence)

Amantadine is a weak uncompetitive NMDA-receptor antagonist; the Gocovri label states that its therapeutic mechanism is unknown and distinguishes anticholinergic-like adverse effects from demonstrated direct anticholinergic activity. (low confidence)

The February 2026 Gocovri label warns against abrupt withdrawal because of worsening parkinsonism and neuropsychiatric symptoms; for treatment longer than 4 weeks it advises, if possible, halving the dose for the final week. (low confidence)

The 2003 Cochrane amantadine review found insufficient evidence for efficacy and safety for general idiopathic Parkinson symptoms from older trials; its searches extended through 2001, so that conclusion does not include the 2017 EASE LID dyskinesia trial. (medium confidence)

The AAN recommends using the lowest effective dopamine-agonist dose and, when stopping treatment because of adverse effects, gradual dose reduction when possible with monitoring for dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome. (low confidence)

Both US apomorphine labels contraindicate concomitant use with ondansetron, listed among serotonin receptor antagonists, because profound hypotension and loss of consciousness have been reported. (medium confidence)

Apomorphine infusion has specific local tolerability burdens: the ONAPGO label warns of infusion-site reactions and infections and instructs daily site changes; it also warns that treatment can cause or worsen dyskinesia. (low confidence)

Dopamine dysregulation syndrome (DDS) involves compulsive use of dopamine replacement medication beyond motor requirements, with drug seeking or hoarding, social impairment and sometimes mood elevation; distress can emerge when doses are reduced. (medium confidence)

Dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome can complicate tapering, with anxiety, panic, depression or dysphoria, fatigue and pain; symptoms may be refractory to levodopa replacement. Its recognition matters because it can prevent successful agonist withdrawal. (medium confidence)

NICE recommends specialist cognitive behavioural therapy directed at ICDs when changing dopaminergic treatment is ineffective. A small randomized waiting-list-controlled trial supports short-term improvement in patient symptom severity. (medium confidence)

A clinical review states that non-pharmacological approaches such as limiting access to credit cards, the Internet or gambling venues should be implemented but are usually not enough on their own; a management table notes that carer involvement in surveillance can facilitate earlier detection of ICDs and that caregivers or family may participate in management when symptoms persist. (medium confidence)
Intestinal levodopa infusion adds procedure and device burdens: DUOPA labeling warns that gastrointestinal procedure-related complications can require surgery or cause death. (low confidence)
COMT inhibition reduces levodopa conversion to 3-O-methyldopa and increases levodopa availability; it is an adjunct mechanism that depends on levodopa treatment. (medium confidence)
Safinamide and opicapone can cause or worsen dyskinesia when added to levodopa; both US labels state that reducing levodopa or another dopaminergic drug may mitigate it. (medium confidence)
Istradefylline is an adenosine A2A receptor antagonist used in the US label as an adjunct to levodopa/carbidopa for adult OFF episodes; its precise therapeutic mechanism is unknown. (low confidence)
Motor fluctuations are transitions between ON, when levodopa provides useful symptomatic benefit, and OFF, when responsive symptoms re-emerge and function declines. (low confidence)
NICE recommendation 1.3.9 advises seeking Parkinson’s specialist advice before modifying therapy when dyskinesia or motor fluctuations, including wearing-off, develop. (low confidence)

NICE advises considering amantadine when dyskinesia is not adequately managed by modifying existing therapy; the Aradi–Hauser review likewise includes it among options for peak-dose dyskinesia. (medium confidence)

The 2025 MDS review assessed OFF-time, ON-time, motor impairment, disability, health-related quality of life and adverse effects; these outcomes should be distinguished when interpreting treatment benefit. (low confidence)

Hospital fasting orders and swallowing difficulties can cause missed medication; the pharmacy review recommends planning alternative administration and obtaining specialist or pharmacist input for enteral conversion when needed. (low confidence)

A pharmacy-informatics review proposes that, when adding a medicine to the hospital formulary is not feasible, the inpatient pharmacy identify patient-owned supplies and have them re-labeled for use during the stay, and it notes that the FDA Orange Book defines therapeutic equivalency; the Parkinson's Foundation safe and contraindicated medications document states that medications, even in the same class, are usually not interchangeable and that patients should be allowed to supply their own medications if not on formulary. (medium confidence)
The pharmacy review reports that high-protein meals can reduce levodopa absorption and suggests coordinating meal delivery with medication times when feasible. (low confidence)

The tremor review states that underdosing of levodopa or non-adherence are important causes of poor tremor control in clinical practice, and that impaired swallowing, altered gastric motility and bacterial overgrowth leading to impaired levodopa absorption may contribute to levodopa pseudoresistance. (medium confidence)

For residual tremor, anticholinergics have only a restricted role in young cognitively intact patients, propranolol has limited supporting evidence, and clozapine may help but requires specialist safety monitoring because of serious adverse effects. (medium confidence)

Freezing treatment studies are difficult to compare when they omit subtype classification or rely on a single rating-scale item; identifying the freezing phenotype and measuring freezing directly are important to interpretation. (medium confidence)

The February 2026 Gocovri label starts treatment at 137 mg at bedtime and increases after one week to 274 mg at bedtime; it explicitly states that Gocovri is not substitutable with other immediate-release or extended-release amantadine products. (low confidence)

DUOPA is carbidopa-levodopa enteral suspension delivered into the jejunum through a PEG-J tube and pump. Its March 2026 label specifies a 16-hour daily infusion, up to 2000 mg levodopa, followed by nighttime oral immediate-release carbidopa-levodopa. (low confidence)

The October 2024 VYALEV label permits infusion during waking hours or for 24 hours, with individualized infusion rates; the maximum recommended daily foslevodopa dose is 3,525 mg, approximately equivalent to 2,500 mg levodopa. (low confidence)

The July 2026 INBRIJA label specifies inhaling two 42 mg capsules (84 mg) per OFF episode, up to five times daily, with a 420 mg daily maximum. Capsules are inhaled using the INBRIJA inhaler and must not be swallowed. (low confidence)

The US XADAGO label uses safinamide as an adjunct to levodopa/carbidopa for OFF episodes: start at 50 mg once daily, with an increase to 100 mg once daily after two weeks according to need and tolerability; doses above 100 mg have no demonstrated added benefit. (low confidence)

Entacapone is given as 200 mg with each levodopa/decarboxylase-inhibitor dose; its short duration adds dosing burden, and reported adverse effects include diarrhea, urine discoloration and dyskinesia. (low confidence)

The US ONGENTYS label recommends opicapone 50 mg once daily at bedtime, without food for one hour before and at least one hour after; moderate hepatic impairment reduces the dose to 25 mg, and severe hepatic impairment calls for avoiding use. (low confidence)

The US NOURIANZ label recommends istradefylline 20 mg once daily, with a possible increase to 40 mg; strong CYP3A4 inhibitors cap dosing at 20 mg, and strong CYP3A4 inducers should be avoided. (low confidence)

EASE LID excluded patients with MMSE scores below 24, estimated glomerular filtration rates below 50 mL/min/1.73 m2, and prior amantadine intolerance or lack of response; these exclusions limit direct generalization to such patients. (low confidence)

Gocovri renal dosing is formulation-specific: the February 2026 label recommends 68.5 mg initially and a maximum of 137 mg daily for moderate impairment, 68.5 mg daily for severe impairment, and contraindicates use in end-stage renal disease below 15 mL/min/1.73 m2. (low confidence)

NICE recommendations tagged 2017 advise against vitamin E as neuroprotective treatment, restrict co-enzyme Q10 neuroprotective use to clinical trials, and advise against creatine supplements in Parkinson disease; these adjunct supplements should not be presented as established neuroprotective therapy. (low confidence) (verified as of 2017-07-19)

The 2021 AAN guideline allows dopamine agonists as initial treatment in selected early-PD patients younger than 60 years who are at higher dyskinesia risk; it advises against their use for initial treatment in those older than 70 years or with preexisting cognitive impairment, excessive daytime sleepiness, or hallucinations. (low confidence)

In the PROUD delayed-start trial, clinical and neuroimaging outcomes did not support a disease-modifying effect of pramipexole, consistent with the AAN guideline assessment of dopamine agonist trials. (medium confidence)

In Parkinson’s disease, clinically important impulse control disorders include compulsive gambling, shopping, sexual behaviour and binge eating; these behaviours can cause serious financial and psychosocial harm. (medium confidence)
Dopamine agonist exposure is a major ICD risk factor, but ICDs can occur with other dopaminergic therapies; absence of agonist treatment does not eliminate risk. (medium confidence)

The French DIGPD longitudinal cohort found independent associations of greater lifetime average dopamine agonist dose and longer exposure with ICDs. This is observational evidence; individual susceptibility and studies with conflicting dose associations limit a universal dose threshold. (medium confidence)

NICE NG71 states that when dopamine agonist therapy is started, people and, as appropriate, their family members and carers should be given oral and written information about the increased risk of impulse control disorders, which may be concealed by the person affected, and that the discussion should be recorded; a clinical review states that all patients with PD should be advised about the potential risk of behavioural addictions, especially following dopamine agonist therapy. (medium confidence)

NICE NG71 states that, if a person with Parkinson's disease has developed a problematic impulse control disorder, advice should be sought from a healthcare professional with specialist expertise in Parkinson's disease before modifying dopaminergic therapy, and describes first gradually reducing the dopamine agonist while monitoring both ICD response and withdrawal; a management review tabulates reducing the oral dopamine agonist while observing for resolution of ICDs, loss of motor control and dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome. (medium confidence)

The CBT trial randomized 27 patients to intervention and 17 to waiting-list control. Its small size, six-month follow-up, inability to blind participants and assessors, and lack of an active control limit certainty; caregiver burden and distress did not improve significantly. (low confidence)

Naltrexone has not established overall efficacy for PD-related ICDs: the 2015 management review reports a negative primary global-response outcome but improved secondary QUIP-RS scores, whereas the 2024 review summarizes the trial as a failure to improve ICDs. Secondary scale improvement should not be represented as definitive treatment success. (medium confidence)

Foscarbidopa and foslevodopa are prodrugs converted in vivo to carbidopa and levodopa. The October 2024 VYALEV label indicates subcutaneous pump infusion for motor fluctuations in adults with advanced Parkinson’s disease. (high confidence)
INBRIJA labeling does not recommend use in asthma, COPD, or other chronic underlying lung disease because of bronchospasm risk; cough is among its common adverse reactions. (low confidence)

Mitsubishi Tanabe Pharma announced on October 23, 2025 that the US FDA had issued a complete response letter for the new drug application of investigational ND0612 for motor fluctuations in people with Parkinson's disease, with FDA observations regarding the manufacturing site and the nonclinical information. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-10-23)

Tanabe Pharma announced that Onerji (project code ND0612), a continuous subcutaneous infusion of liquid levodopa/carbidopa, received European Commission marketing authorization on April 27 (local time) for motor fluctuations in advanced Parkinson's disease not sufficiently controlled by oral anti-Parkinson medicinal products; the NeuroDerm news listing dates that announcement April 30, 2026. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-04-30)
Selegiline and rasagiline can provide modest symptomatic benefit as monotherapy in early Parkinson’s disease. (low confidence)

ADAGIO found a possible disease-modifying signal at 1 mg/day but not 2 mg/day and urged caution, while the clinical review reports that long-term follow-up did not confirm disease modification. (medium confidence)

Wearing-off is gradual loss of dose benefit before the next dose; sudden OFF can be unrelated to dose timing, delayed ON means unusually slow benefit after a dose, and dose failure means no benefit from that dose. These are distinct response patterns. (low confidence)

NICE advises against deep brain stimulation when best medical therapy adequately controls symptoms, and recommends considering it when advanced disease is not adequately controlled; the MDS review also describes escalation when less invasive options provide insufficient benefit. (medium confidence)

NICE NG71 states that people with Parkinson's disease who are admitted to hospital or care homes should have their medicines given at the appropriate times, which in some cases may mean allowing self-medication, and adjusted by, or only after discussion with, a specialist in the management of Parkinson's disease; a pharmacy-informatics review describes electronic order entry that can mistranscribe a patient's specific medication times and intervals. (medium confidence)

NICE advises against abrupt withdrawal or sudden failure of antiparkinsonian treatment from poor absorption because of the risk of acute akinesia or neuroleptic malignant syndrome; drug holidays should not be used. (low confidence)

A pharmacy-informatics review states that medications affecting dopaminergic states must be used cautiously in Parkinson's disease, and singles out dopamine antagonists in the antipsychotic class (including haloperidol) and the antiemetic class (including metoclopramide, promethazine and prochlorperazine) as able to worsen Parkinson motor function. (medium confidence)

The methylphenidate gait trial report states that dopaminergic treatments and currently available surgical therapies are often insufficiently effective for gait disorders in PD, and NICE NG71 recommends offering Parkinson's disease-specific physiotherapy for people experiencing balance or motor function problems. (medium confidence)

ReSPonD was a phase 2 trial in people with Parkinson disease who had fallen, could walk unaided and did not have dementia: rivastigmine improved step-time variability during normal walking and a simple dual task, but not the complex dual task, and caused more gastrointestinal adverse effects. (low confidence)

In the 2017 EASE LID trial, the week 12 placebo-adjusted improvement in Unified Dyskinesia Rating Scale score was 7.9 points. This is evidence for the studied extended-release product and population, rather than proof that every amantadine formulation is equivalent. (medium confidence)

In the 12-week randomized TOLEDO trial, apomorphine infusion reduced daily OFF time by 2·47 hours versus 0·58 hours with placebo, a between-group difference of 1·89 hours (95% CI 0·62–3·16 hours favoring apomorphine); six apomorphine-treated participants withdrew because of treatment-related adverse events. (low confidence)

In DIGPD, among 306 participants without baseline ICDs who had follow-up, estimated cumulative ICD incidence over five years was 46.1% (95% CI 37.4–55.7): 51.5% in ever dopamine-agonist users versus 12.4% in never users. These are cohort-specific cumulative incidences, not a general population prevalence or a DDS estimate. (low confidence)

Previous impulsive or addictive behaviour, alcohol or smoking history, and younger age are described as risk factors for ICDs in Parkinson's disease; these are risk associations rather than diagnostic rules. (medium confidence)
Conversion from immediate-release carbidopa-levodopa to CREXONT is not a 1:1 dose substitution; use formulation-specific conversion and titration rather than matching milligrams. (high confidence)

In RISE-PD, 506 participants were randomized; IPX203 increased daily good ON time by a least-squares mean 0.53 hours versus immediate-release carbidopa-levodopa (95% CI 0.09–0.97), with mean dosing approximately three versus five times daily. Good ON meant ON without troublesome dyskinesia. (low confidence)

RISE-PD compared IPX203 with immediate-release carbidopa-levodopa in patients already experiencing fluctuations. It did not establish efficacy in early PD versus placebo or prevention of later motor complications; protocol dosing was limited to no more often than every 6 hours. (low confidence)

VYALEV’s pivotal-study safety data in the October 2024 label report infusion-site reactions in 62% versus 8% with placebo infusion and site infections in 28% versus 3%; adverse reactions led to VYALEV discontinuation in 22%. These are study-specific rates, not comparisons against intestinal infusion. (low confidence)
Inhaled levodopa (INBRIJA) is an intermittent treatment for OFF episodes in patients already treated with carbidopa/levodopa, rather than a stand-alone maintenance formulation. (high confidence)

In the foslevodopa-foscarbidopa phase 3 trial, continuous subcutaneous infusion improved ON time without troublesome dyskinesia and reduced OFF time compared with oral immediate-release levodopa-carbidopa, but infusion-site events were frequent and more participants discontinued treatment because of adverse events. (low confidence)

Safinamide adjunct trials support reduced OFF time and increased ON time without troublesome dyskinesia; the MDS review describes benefits around one hour compared with placebo, although individual trials vary. (medium confidence)

When dyskinesia and OFF coexist on immediate-release carbidopa–levodopa, smaller individual doses given more frequently (fractionation) may help reduce peak–trough fluctuations; this is an option rather than a guaranteed response. (low confidence)

For fluctuations inadequately controlled by oral medication, infusion therapies can be considered; the MDS review supports selected continuous-delivery treatments as likely efficacious, rather than guaranteeing benefit for every patient. (medium confidence)

The February 2026 Gocovri label indicates this extended-release amantadine product for dyskinesia during levodopa-based treatment and as adjunctive treatment for off episodes; these are product-specific indications. (low confidence)
Hallucinations, peripheral edema and dizziness were prominent adverse events in EASE LID; Gocovri prescribing information also lists these adverse reactions. (medium confidence)

The February 2026 Gocovri label warns that concomitant drugs with anticholinergic properties may potentiate anticholinergic-like adverse effects; it advises reducing the anticholinergic drug or Gocovri dose if atropine-like effects appear. (low confidence)

Benztropine and trihexyphenidyl are anticholinergic options used particularly in younger patients; cognitive impairment, confusion, hallucinations, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation and urinary retention restrict their usefulness, especially with advancing age. (medium confidence)

The Parkinson Foundation describes anticholinergics as predominantly useful for tremor with little effect on other symptoms; the Cochrane review found motor benefit over placebo but conflicting results and insufficient support for a preferential effect on tremor. The latter limits claims of established symptom selectivity. (medium confidence)

For early PD, the AAN review found greater motor improvement with initial levodopa than with initial dopamine agonists, while initial agonists caused less dyskinesia during the first five years; severe or disabling dyskinesia was uncommon in that interval. (low confidence)

The AAN found no strong evidence favoring ropinirole over pramipexole or extended-release over immediate-release pramipexole for early-PD motor efficacy; formulation, administration route, cost, and patient preferences should guide selection. (low confidence)

Dopamine agonists require monitoring for daytime somnolence, sudden sleep onset, hallucinations, nausea, and orthostatic hypotension; these are also explicit apomorphine-label safety concerns. (medium confidence)

APOKYN prescribing information revised January 2025 describes subcutaneous apomorphine for acute, intermittent treatment of OFF episodes in advanced PD and requires the first dose under medical supervision. (low confidence)

ONAPGO prescribing information revised May 2026 describes subcutaneous infusion for motor fluctuations in adults with advanced PD; it explicitly states that ONAPGO is not substitutable for apomorphine products intended for intermittent use. (low confidence)

A 2024 clinical review distinguishes DDS management from usual ICD management: DDS may require reducing levodopa or fast-acting apomorphine exposure, with monitoring for motor deterioration and withdrawal and sometimes inpatient multidisciplinary care. This is review guidance, not evidence of a proven universally effective regimen. (low confidence)

Levodopa is converted to dopamine in the brain. Carbidopa inhibits peripheral levodopa decarboxylation, increasing levodopa availability to the brain and reducing peripheral nausea and vomiting; it does not remove central levodopa adverse effects. (high confidence)

Oral carbidopa-levodopa is supplied as immediate-release tablets, controlled-release tablets, and extended-release capsules; the Parkinson’s Foundation describes Rytary as containing beads absorbed at different rates. (low confidence)

Fewer dosing occasions did not mean fewer pills in RISE-PD: mean daily pill counts were 10.6 with IPX203 and 8.7 with immediate-release treatment, with the trial restricted to one strength of each formulation. (low confidence)

The December 2019 Rytary prescribing information instructs patients not to chew, divide or crush the capsules; for difficulty swallowing, it permits opening a capsule and immediately consuming its entire contents sprinkled on applesauce. (low confidence)

BouNDless studied ND0612 as continuous subcutaneous levodopa-carbidopa solution, with supplemental oral levodopa-carbidopa if needed; its randomized phase followed open-label optimization of both regimens. (low confidence)

BouNDless reported more ON time without troublesome dyskinesia with ND0612 than with oral levodopa-carbidopa, while infusion-site reactions were its most common adverse events; the study findings should not be treated as a statement of regulatory approval. (low confidence)

A NeuroDerm news page carries Tanabe Pharma's announcement of its decision to wind down the operations of its wholly owned subsidiary NeuroDerm Ltd., the company developing ND0612. (medium confidence)
Selegiline and rasagiline inhibit MAO-B irreversibly, whereas safinamide inhibits it reversibly. (low confidence)

Safinamide inhibits MAO-B and thereby reduces dopamine catabolism; additional effects on glutamate release and sodium channels have been described, but their added clinical relevance remains uncertain. (medium confidence)

Rasagiline reduces OFF time as an adjunct; the MDS review describes placebo-adjusted reductions of 0.5–0.9 hours/day and rates it likely efficacious, while noting that the average OFF-time improvement did not meet its clinical-meaningfulness threshold. (medium confidence)

The MDS review found insufficient evidence for selegiline specifically as treatment of motor fluctuations despite attempted optimal oral levodopa therapy, citing small samples, low-quality evidence and heterogeneous results; this conclusion is scoped to that indication. (low confidence)
Entacapone and opicapone act peripherally, while tolcapone crosses the blood–brain barrier and inhibits COMT centrally as well as peripherally. (low confidence)
Opicapone has placebo-controlled evidence for reducing OFF time; the MDS review found no significant PDQ-39 improvement in its included trials. (medium confidence)

Tolcapone’s practical role is restricted by potentially fatal liver injury and the need for regular liver-function monitoring; the clinical review describes its use after inadequate response or intolerance to other COMT inhibitors. (low confidence)

Safinamide has drug-specific interaction restrictions: its US label contraindicates other MAO inhibitors, including linezolid, selected opioids such as tramadol, SNRIs and certain other antidepressants, and dextromethorphan; SSRIs instead require the lowest effective dose and monitoring for serotonin syndrome. (low confidence)

Istradefylline’s non-dopaminergic receptor target does not eliminate dyskinesia or psychiatric adverse effects: the US label warns of worsened dyskinesia and hallucinations and advises against treatment in major psychotic disorders. (low confidence)

Evidence assessments differ for istradefylline: the MDS motor-fluctuation review rates it likely efficacious while noting inconsistent effects of unclear clinical relevance, whereas EMA’s Nouryant refusal assessment found efficacy insufficiently established. These attributed judgments should not be collapsed into a universal efficacy or availability claim. (medium confidence)

Peak-dose dyskinesia occurs at the peak of the levodopa response; diphasic dyskinesia occurs as levodopa levels rise and fall. Painful dystonia can also occur during OFF, particularly early morning OFF. (low confidence)

A common initial strategy for wearing-off is to shorten the interval between levodopa doses. Practical schedule adjustments are widely used, but the 2025 MDS review notes that not all have been tested in randomized trials. (medium confidence)

For dyskinesia without OFF time, the Aradi–Hauser review suggests considering lower individual levodopa doses or reducing adjunctive medication. This recommendation is explicitly for that response pattern. (low confidence)

If schedule adjustments do not sufficiently improve motor fluctuations, additional medical treatment may be needed; persistent inadequate control can prompt consideration of pump therapy or a neurosurgical procedure. (medium confidence)

NICE NG71 lists the person's individual clinical circumstances (for example symptoms, comorbidities and risks from polypharmacy), their lifestyle circumstances, preferences, needs and goals, and the potential benefits and harms of the different drug classes among its considerations in choosing treatment; the MDS review states that safety and individual tolerability must be taken into account together with each patient's preference. (medium confidence)

The 2025 MDS review used a literature search conducted on January 1, 2023 and required randomized trials with at least three months of follow-up. Its evidence conclusions are therefore bounded by that search and eligibility criteria. (low confidence)

The 2025 MDS review explicitly states that its efficacy designations do not prioritize treatment order or establish larger benefit for an “efficacious” treatment than for a “likely efficacious” treatment. It also notes few long-term comparative studies to guide the first treatment choice. (low confidence)

The MDS review illustrates that OFF-time reduction does not necessarily translate into a clinically meaningful improvement in disability or quality of life: its extended-release levodopa comparison improved OFF/ON outcomes but did not reach clinical relevance for those broader outcomes. (low confidence)

The motor-complications review describes no significant difference in motor-complication rates at 80 weeks in a trial comparing immediate levodopa initiation with a 40-week delay; this finding does not establish that longer delays prevent complications. (low confidence)

NICE advises that hospital or care-home medication changes should be made by, or discussed with, a Parkinson specialist, and that appropriate dose timing may sometimes require self-medication. (low confidence)

A pharmacy workflow review recommends treating levodopa as time-critical, documenting administration times and reasons for deviations, and using overdue alerts and custom order times. Its proposed 30-minute window is an operational recommendation, not proof that every patient can safely tolerate that delay. (low confidence)

A pharmacy-informatics review states that pharmacist medication reconciliation involves checking dose, route, frequency and timing against the home regimen, with confirmation from the patient, care partner or outpatient records. (low confidence)

The Parkinson Foundation advises updating a written medication form whenever the routine changes and keeping a supply of current medicines in labeled pharmacy bottles for hospital use. (low confidence)

NICE limits its discussion of protein redistribution to people taking levodopa who experience motor fluctuations, and specifically advises against reducing total daily protein intake. (low confidence)

The APOKYN label contraindicates concomitant use of apomorphine with ondansetron, listed among serotonin receptor antagonists, following reports of profound hypotension and loss of consciousness. (low confidence)

The Foundation hospital checklist warns about mixing MAO-B inhibitors with listed pain medicines and calls for consultation among the Parkinson clinician, surgeon and anesthesiologist; this checklist does not establish identical interaction risks for every listed agent. (low confidence)

The Foundation cautions that benzodiazepines and other medicines for sleep or pain can contribute to confusion, hallucinations and falls; its acute-agitation advice limits repeated benzodiazepine use to avoid worsening confusion. (low confidence)

Observational findings on medication delays and hospital length of stay conflict: Martinez-Ramirez and colleagues reported longer stays with delayed or missed doses, whereas Skelly and colleagues found no adjusted association; these findings do not establish that delays invariably prolong admission. (medium confidence)

Disabling tremor that persists despite optimized medication can justify specialist assessment for invasive treatment, including deep brain stimulation; the tremor review also identifies focused ultrasound as an option. (medium confidence)

Freezing is heterogeneous: OFF freezing usually improves with dopaminergic treatment, pseudo-ON freezing can improve with additional dopamine, and true ON freezing can be induced by dopaminergic stimulation; these categories should not be assumed to respond identically. (low confidence)

For OFF-related freezing, reducing OFF time through individualized dopaminergic treatment is a first-line approach; the German guideline recommends levodopa for symptomatic freezing treatment. (medium confidence)
The ReSPonD investigators interpreted rivastigmine as potentially improving gait stability and possibly reducing falls, and explicitly called for phase 3 confirmation. (medium confidence)

In the Espay randomized crossover trial, methylphenidate did not improve gait and tended to worsen motor function, sleepiness and quality of life; this negative trial limits extrapolation from positive open-label observations. (medium confidence)

The German consensus guideline allows methylphenidate to be considered for freezing, whereas the Espay trial authors report no gait benefit and a tendency toward worse outcomes; this is a difference between a permissive recommendation and a negative trial in a specific population. (medium confidence)

narrative.documentConcept: Amantadine, anticholinergics and other adjunct drugs
narrative.text: Amantadine has formulation-specific evidence for dyskinesia, while its precise therapeutic mechanism remains unknown. Extended-release Gocovri requires attention to renal function, hallucinations, edema and withdrawal. Anticholinergics such as benztropine and trihexyphenidyl have a restricted role because cognitive and peripheral adverse effects can outweigh motor benefit, especially in older people. Clinical emphasis on tremor should be distinguished from the weak trial evidence for preferential tremor efficacy. Older inconclusive amantadine reviews address different evidence from later formulation-specific trials. NICE discourages several proposed neuroprotective supplements.

narrative.documentConcept: Amantadine, anticholinergics and other adjunct drugs
narrative.text: The Parkinson Foundation describes anticholinergics as predominantly useful for tremor with little effect on other symptoms; the Cochrane review found motor benefit over placebo but conflicting results and insufficient support for a preferential effect on tremor. The latter limits claims of established symptom selectivity.

narrative.documentConcept: Dopamine agonists and apomorphine
narrative.text: Dopamine agonists offer symptomatic treatment for selected patients with Parkinson disease. Early-treatment choices require balancing motor benefit against sleepiness, hallucinations, and orthostatic hypotension; formulation choice should reflect patient preferences and tolerability. Apomorphine has distinct intermittent subcutaneous rescue and continuous infusion uses in advanced disease. The TOLEDO randomized trial supports infusion for persistent motor fluctuations, but adverse effects and treatment withdrawal remain relevant. Product-specific supervision, contraindications, and infusion-site care are essential. The PROUD trial did not support disease modification by pramipexole.

narrative.documentConcept: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation
narrative.text: Impulse control disorders in Parkinson’s disease include harmful gambling, shopping, sexual behaviour and binge eating. Dopamine dysregulation syndrome involves compulsive medication overuse; punding involves repetitive, purposeless activity. Dopamine agonists carry a major ICD risk, although other dopaminergic therapy can also be implicated. Prevention requires candid patient and family counselling and repeated behavioural review. Management generally starts with specialist-guided gradual agonist reduction, while watching motor control and withdrawal. DDS can require a different medication-reduction strategy. Specialist cognitive behavioural therapy may help persistent ICDs, but trial limitations and endpoint-dependent drug results argue against overstating treatment certainty.

narrative.documentConcept: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation
narrative.text: Naltrexone interpretation depends on the endpoint: the 2015 review describes a negative primary outcome with secondary QUIP-RS improvement, while the 2024 review summarizes failure to improve ICDs. These are different readings of the same trial, not independent efficacy replications.

narrative.text: Which DDS treatment strategies have the strongest comparative evidence beyond expert clinical review?

narrative.documentConcept: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation
narrative.text: What is the durability of benefit from specialist CBT in larger trials with active controls?

narrative.documentConcept: Levodopa and carbidopa formulations and delivery
narrative.text: Levodopa supplies the dopamine precursor, while carbidopa reduces peripheral conversion and associated nausea. Delivery options include immediate- and controlled-release tablets, extended-release capsules, intestinal carbidopa-levodopa infusion, subcutaneous foscarbidopa/foslevodopa infusion, and intermittent inhaled levodopa. Extended-release oral formulations aim to sustain benefit with fewer dosing occasions, but conversion requires formulation-specific titration. Infusions can provide sustained delivery while adding tube, pump, procedure, or skin-site burdens. Inhaled levodopa addresses OFF episodes alongside existing carbidopa/levodopa treatment. RISE-PD supports IPX203 over immediate-release treatment in patients with fluctuations; it does not establish prevention of future motor complications. Product-specific labels distinguish routes, dose equivalence, and delivery limitations. Regulatory status of subcutaneous ND0612 is time-sensitive: a US complete response letter was announced on October 23, 2025, and EU marketing authorization was announced in April 2026.

narrative.text: What later label changes and jurisdiction-specific availability apply to CREXONT and VYALEV?

narrative.text: Whether a further US FDA submission or commercial availability of ND0612 follows NeuroDerm's announced wind-down is not stated in the sources read; the wind-down announcement text read carries no date, although a news list on the same page runs through April 30, 2026.

narrative.documentConcept: MAO-B, COMT inhibitors and adenosine A2A antagonists
narrative.text: MAO-B inhibitors preserve dopamine activity; COMT inhibitors prolong levodopa availability; istradefylline targets adenosine A2A receptors. These classes offer distinct adjunct approaches to OFF episodes, with modest and drug-dependent benefits. Selegiline and rasagiline also have early-disease symptomatic evidence, but rasagiline disease modification is unconfirmed. Safinamide and opicapone have supportive adjunct trials, while istradefylline evidence assessments differ between the MDS review and EMA’s refusal assessment. Selection requires attention to dosing burden, hepatic function, interactions and dyskinesia. Tolcapone carries a serious liver-injury concern. Receptor selectivity does not remove psychiatric or dyskinesia risks. The claims distinguish symptom improvement from disease modification and diary-time benefit from quality-of-life improvement.

narrative.documentConcept: MAO-B, COMT inhibitors and adenosine A2A antagonists
narrative.text: The MDS review rates istradefylline likely efficacious but notes inconsistent benefit of unclear clinical relevance; EMA’s Nouryant refusal assessment found efficacy not established. These are explicitly attributed judgments from distinct assessments.

narrative.documentConcept: Motor fluctuations, wearing-off and dyskinesia management
narrative.text: Motor fluctuations divide the day into periods of useful medication benefit (ON) and returning symptoms (OFF). Wearing-off, delayed ON, sudden OFF and dose failure represent different patterns; peak-dose and diphasic dyskinesia also differ in their timing. Management requires specialist assessment and balancing symptom control against involuntary movements. Common approaches include adjusting dose intervals, reducing individual doses when appropriate, and escalating treatment when control remains inadequate. Coexisting dyskinesia and OFF may require fractionation rather than simply reducing medication. Patient goals, tolerability, disability and quality of life matter alongside time-based outcomes. The 2025 MDS evidence categories describe strength of evidence and should not be interpreted as a treatment sequence.

narrative.documentConcept: PD medication timing, interactions and hospital safety
narrative.text: Medication safety in Parkinson disease depends on preserving individualized dose times, avoiding abrupt interruption, planning administration during fasting or swallowing problems, and checking medicines that block dopamine or interact with the existing regimen. NICE and hospital safety resources emphasize appropriate timing, specialist involvement and accurate medication records. Pharmacy recommendations address reconciliation, custom order times, alerts, medicine availability and careful substitution. Protein redistribution requires nutritional safeguards. Antiemetic choice must account for drug-specific contraindications. Observational evidence about whether medication delays prolong hospital stay is conflicting, so hospital length-of-stay findings should not be presented as universal causal effects.

narrative.documentConcept: Tremor, gait, freezing and postural instability management
narrative.text: Tremor and axial disability require symptom-specific assessment. Levodopa is the principal drug approach for troublesome tremor, and apparent resistance can reflect inadequate treatment delivery. Persistent disabling tremor can warrant specialist invasive-treatment assessment. Freezing must be assessed in relation to medication state: OFF, pseudo-ON and true ON freezing need different interpretations. Reducing OFF time may help OFF freezing, but persistent gait and balance problems also require Parkinson-specific physiotherapy. Rivastigmine gait findings are promising phase 2 evidence rather than established freezing treatment. Methylphenidate evidence is inconsistent, with a negative randomized trial despite permissive consensus guidance.

narrative.documentConcept: Tremor, gait, freezing and postural instability management
narrative.text: The German guideline permits consideration of methylphenidate for freezing; the Espay randomized trial reports no gait benefit and a tendency toward worse outcomes. These positions concern different levels of evidence and do not establish uniform benefit.
